Juventus endured its worst domestic season since 1990–91, superstar Alessandro Del Piero on 8 November 1998, picked up a serious knee injury in the final minutes of a 2–2 draw with Udinese;[2] and a backlash for France's World Cup hero Zinedine Zidane. In December, Lippi announced his departure in June to manage Inter the next season and in February Lippi was let go by the club, with successful former Parma coach Carlo Ancelotti taking over.

With Ancelotti at the helm, Juve managed to salvage some respectability by reaching the semi-finals of the Champions League, then, playmaker Zidane limped off at half-time in Juventus's draw at home to Bologna on 12 April 1999 ending his campaign, just before the second leg against eventual champions Manchester United defeating Juventus 3-2 at Delle Alpi.

The knee has been troubling him for a month where eventual champions Manchester United just got the better of the Italian champions. But following that narrow defeat, Juventus had to settle for the UEFA Cup the next season, due to a lowly seventh place in the league.

The Brazil national football team (Portuguese: Seleção Brasileira de Futebol) represents Brazil in men's international football and is administered by the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF), the governing body for football in Brazil. They have been a member of FIFA since 1923 and a member of CONMEBOL since 1916.


Brazil is the most successful national team in the FIFA World Cup, being crowned winner five times: 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994 and 2002. The Seleção also has the best overall performance in the World Cup competition, both in proportional and absolute terms.


Brazil is the only national team to have won the World Cup on four different continents: once in Europe (1958 Sweden), once in South America (1962 Chile), twice in North America (1970 Mexico and 1994 United States) and once in Asia (2002 Korea/Japan). They share with France and Argentina the feat to have won the three most important men's football titles overseen by FIFA: the World Cup, the Confederations Cup, and the Olympic tournament. They also share with Spain a record of 35 consecutive matches undefeated.

Following a net-buster from Daniele De Rossi and a cool finish from Eric Abidal, Del Piero stepped up to the mark and a calm and collected second later the ball was in the back of the net. This is the fully-customizable short-sleeve home kit for AS Roma’s 2000-2001 season.

AS Roma fans still remember the 2000-2001 season as if it happened yesterday. It was a season where Roma won the title, taking it away from the reigning champions, and their most hated rival, Lazio.

This was only Roma’s third title, first in 19 years, and the last one to this day. It’s no surprise they won the title when you look at the players who wore this jersey; Cafu, Zebina, Walter Samuel, Tomassi, Totti, and the key who unlocked the title – Gabriel Batistuta, also known as Gabigol. Batistuta was the team’s leading goalscorer with 20 league goals.

Batigol also scored one of the most emotional goals ever, as he banged in a shot from 20 meters to Fiorentina’s net; Fiorentina was the love of Bati’s life, and just after scoring, Batistuta took down in tears as he hurt the one he loved the most. This, however, did help at the end of the season, when Roma won the title by just two points ahead of Juventus. Roma did deserve the title, as they only conceded three losses during the entire season.

Notable Players: Francesco Totti, Gabriel Batistuta, Vincenzo Montella, Cafu, Emerson, Walter Samuel, Hidetoshi Nakata, Damiano Tommasi, Marco Delvecchio

STORY :

Football Club Internazionale Milano, commonly referred to as Internazionale (pronounced [ˌinternattsjoˈnaːle]) or simply Inter, and known as Inter Milan outside Italy,[9][10] is an Italian professional football club based in Milan, Lombardy. Inter is the only Italian club never to have been relegated from the top flight of Italian football.

Founded in 1908 following a schism within the Milan Cricket and Football Club (now A.C. Milan), Inter won its first championship in 1910. Since its formation, the club has won 30 domestic trophies, including 18 league titles, 7 Coppa Italia and 5 Supercoppa Italiana. From 2006 to 2010, the club won five successive league titles, equalling the all-time record at that time.[11] They have won the Champions League three times: two back-to-back in 1964 and 1965 and then another in 2010. Their latest win completed an unprecedented Italian seasonal treble, with Inter winning the Coppa Italia and the Scudetto the same year.[12] The club has also won three UEFA Cups, two Intercontinental Cups and one FIFA Club World Cup

STORY :

This is the fully-customizable short-sleeve home kit for the Juventus 2002-2003 season.

This kit represents a special (and also heartbreaking) season for the Bianconeri as Juve won the Scudetto but lost in the Champions League final against Milan on penalties. Under the guidance of Marcello Lippi, the Bianconeri dominated Italian football in this shirt, as they won the Serie A with a 7-point advance on second-placed Inter, all in the late golden age of the Serie A.

In the Champions League, they dominated the first group stage against Newcastle, Dynamo Kyiv and Feyenoord. Then, they got lucky in the second group stage, as they placed second behind Manchester United, but with the same amount of points (7) as Basel and Deportivo La Coruña, the third and fourth-placed teams. They advanced because of their better goal average. In the quarters, they were drawn against Barcelona, whom they beat in a second leg away from home with the score of 2-1, after a 1-1 draw at home. In the semi-finals, they beat the other Spanish giants Real Madrid, returning a 2-1 win in the first leg with a 3-1 win in the second leg. In the final, they ended up losing against AC Milan in a boring match which finished 0-0, which caused tragedy in the ranks of the Bianconeri.

Notable Players: Alessandro Del Piero, Pavel Nedved, Gianluigi Buffon, Mauro Camoranesi, Marco Di Vaio, Edgar Davids, Gianluca Zambrotta, Lilian Thuram, Alessio Tacchinardi, Ciro Ferrara

STORY :

Italy reached the final of the 1994 USA World Cup after an impressive campaign through the knockout stages, which included a thrilling 2-1 Quarter-Final win over Spain. They were disappointed to ultimately lose the 1994 World Cup final to Brazil, in a penalty shootout that ended 2-3. The marquee players from Italy’s 1994 World Cup team that wore this kit include Franco Baresi, Paolo Maldini, and Roberto Baggio. 

Italy’s national football team are known as the Azzuri for their distinct blue kits. The Italian football federation unveiled a new badge with this shirt; the badge features a leaning rectangle and circle that combine to form a lowercase “i” for Italy. The badge is displayed prominently on the chest and its outline is also woven throughout the fabric of the shirt. Along the collar and trim of each sleeve, red, white, and green triangles pay homage to the Italian flag. 

This jersey has been remade with impeccable attention to detail. It features the same collar, sleeving, ridges and embroidery as the original.

Printing is done in the original style, as close to the authentic font and colour as possible. If the jersey originally had the number printed on the front we will print this unless instructed otherwise.

Please check the measurements carefully as most people find they require a size up. The jerseys have a slim or muscle fit.
